newsitem.title: USA: U.S. air cargo yields seen lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. air cargo yields seen lower.

text.p: U.S. air freight activity will rise sharply but cargo capacity will rise even faster, causing a further erosion of yields, says a forecast by The Colography Group.
The cargo consultancy is forecasting 14.2 percent growth for domestic air freight traffic this year and 13.5 percent growth for U.S. air export shipments.
Revenues will rise by double digit amounts, it said in a statement.

Average yields for ex-U.S. air freight will drop to $4.62 a pound from $4.83 a pound, with the result that "cost control, not price increases, will be the order of the day for carriers in the U.S. and overseas in 1997."
Within the U.S., the downward pressure on yields will be exacerbated by the increasing use of lowcost e-mail and fax services.
Air freight's domestic growth will occur at the expense of less than truckload (LTL) and ground parcel sectors "as more shippers defect from surface products and move up to air", it said.

"In our view, the stagnation of the LTL market isn't caused by economic factors, bad weather or labour disputes," said Colography Group president Ted Scherk. "It is due to a fundamental shift in customer buying habits.

"Increasingly, buyers of transportation services are gravitating to air freight because they perceive it to be a superior value. This trend has been in place for several years, and we see no reversal any time soon."
Integrated carriers like DHL Worldwide Express, FedEx and UPS will boost their export shipments
